author: Rahul kp
topic: Break-Even Point and Margin of Safety
title: Break-Even Point
simple_words: BEP is the sales level where contribution just covers fixed cost. Sales above it is the safety cushion.

definitions.meaning: The level of sales (units or ₹) at which total contribution equals total fixed cost, so profit is zero.
Excess of actual (or budgeted) sales over break-even sales. It shows how far sales can fall before a loss starts.

key_points: At BEP: ==Contribution== = Fixed cost, so profit is nil
Above BEP, each extra unit adds its contribution to profit
Below BEP, the business runs at a loss
!!BEP uses contribution, not profit, in the formula!!

formulas.name: BEP in units
formulas.legend: F = total fixed cost; C per unit = selling price per unit − variable cost per unit

formulas.name: BEP in sales value
formulas.legend: P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales, written as a fraction or %. Use the same ratio form in the formula.

formulas.name: Margin of Safety ratio
formulas.legend: Both sales figures in the same unit, either units or ₹. Denominator is actual sales.

insight.text: Margin of safety in ₹ also equals profit divided by the P/V ratio, a quick check in MCQs.

memory_trick.explanation: Picture a boat (Fixed cost) floating on water (Contribution). Fixed cost always goes on top, contribution below: F over C for units, F over P/V for ₹.

steps: Find P/V ratio if ₹ is asked
Divide fixed cost by C or P/V
exam_tip: Check the unit asked: units or ₹. Then match the denominator, contribution per unit for units, P/V ratio for ₹.

doubt.question: Does P/V ratio change if fixed cost rises?
doubt.answer: No. P/V ratio depends only on selling price and variable cost. A rise in fixed cost raises BEP but leaves P/V ratio unchanged.

mistakes.wrong: Dividing fixed cost by selling price per unit
mistakes.right: Divide fixed cost by contribution per unit (selling price − variable cost per unit).
MoS ratio = (Actual sales − BEP sales) ÷ Actual sales × 100.

mistakes.wrong: Using total variable cost instead of per unit variable cost for contribution per unit
mistakes.right: Use variable cost per unit when finding contribution per unit.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing units and ₹ in the MoS formula
mistakes.right: Take both actual sales and BEP sales in units, or both in ₹.

check_notes: Checker 1: Formula 2 legend: 'written as a fraction or %. Use the same ratio form in the formula' is vague. A student could divide F by 40 instead of 40%. Better wording: 'P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales. If it is given as a %, convert it to a decimal or fraction before dividing (e.g. F ÷ 0.40, not F ÷ 40).'
Checker 1: Step 5: 'Divide MoS by actual sales' leaves out the ×100 that formula 3 has. Better wording: 'Divide MoS by actual sales and multiply by 100 to get MoS %.'

Checker 2: trick_hook 'F over C, always!' is slightly loose: for ₹ the denominator is the P/V ratio, not C per unit. Better: 'F over C (or P/V), always!'. This is wording polish only, and the explanation already gives the correct rule.
